introduction: The alchemists looked for an elixir that would turn base metal into gold. The guide takes their word and gives it to the Word of God, the Holy Spirit and love: these are what change a dull or hostile nature into a new one. Its eighteen quotations are read here with eighteen from elsewhere. Scripture supplies the same change without the laboratory: Saul turned into another man, a stony heart replaced by a heart of flesh, scarlet made white as snow, unlearned men recognised as having been with Jesus, evil deeds changed to good. Herbert, Hopkins and Shakespeare keep the alchemist’s vocabulary of tincture, diamond and gilding. Donne calls the whole art imposture, Jeremiah asks whether the leopard can change his spots, Kant doubts that crooked timber can be made straight, and Bacon suggests that the digging mattered more than the gold. They are set where the guide makes its largest claims, so that a reader can ask what would count as evidence for them.
questions: The guide says that nothing short of a mystic transformation could explain the change in the first believers. What changes in a person would you accept as evidence of such a power?
Jeremiah and Kant doubt that human nature can be remade. What in the guide, or in the scriptures beside it, answers them?
The Qur'an says God does not change a people until they change what is in their hearts. How do grace and effort meet in the image of an elixir?
Bacon's sons found no gold and had a great vintage from the digging. What might be gained from seeking transformation even before it is found?

outside.why: Herbert borrows the alchemist's word too: nothing is so mean that the tincture 'for Thy sake' will not make it grow bright and clean.
Donne calls it imposture all: no chemic ever got the elixir, though he glorifies his pot for some odoriferous thing found by the way. What makes the guide's elixir more than the alchemist's hope?
Samuel tells Saul that the Spirit of the Lord will come upon him and he shall be turned into another man.
Ezekiel hears the promise of a new heart and a new spirit, the stony heart taken away and a heart of flesh given.

Jeremiah asks whether the Ethiopian can change his skin or the leopard his spots, and whether those accustomed to do evil can do good. Is his question despair of change, or a statement of what only a greater power can do?
Jesus answers a like doubt: with men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.
The council marvels at the boldness of unlearned and ignorant men, and takes knowledge that they had been with Jesus.
Paul reminds his converts of what they had been: such were some of you, but ye are washed, sanctified and justified.
Isaiah promises a change of colour past all dyeing: sins as scarlet shall be white as snow, and red like crimson shall be as wool.
Kant held that out of such crooked material as man is made of, nothing can be hammered quite straight. What would he make of the transformations the guide describes?
Job trusts that when he has been tried he shall come forth as gold.
Malachi's refiner sits and purifies as with fire, purging like gold and silver.
Paul speaks of being changed into the same image, from glory to glory, by the Spirit of the Lord.
Hopkins sees poor potsherd and matchwood become, in a flash, immortal diamond.
The Qur'an says of the one who repents, believes and does righteous work that God will change their evil deeds to good deeds.
Shakespeare's morning sun kisses the meadows with golden face and gilds pale streams with heavenly alchemy.
The Qur'an says that God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in their hearts. How do a power that transmutes and a people who must first change fit together?
Bacon compares alchemy to the sons who dug the whole vineyard for buried gold. If the search itself is what bears fruit, what is the elixir a symbol of?

matthew-with-god-all-things-are-possible.text: But Jesus beheld them, and said unto them, With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible

corinthians-such-were-some-of-you.text: And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God

herbert-his-tincture-for-thy-sake.text: All may of Thee partake: / Nothing can be so mean, / Which with his tincture 'for Thy Sake,' / Will not grow bright and clean
herbert-his-tincture-for-thy-sake.author: George Herbert
